question: 80 year old patient from a nursing home. Presents sepsis of urinary origin that does not respond to empiric treatment with ceftriaxone. In the blood cultures and urocultures, E. coli resistant to cephalosporins grows. The laboratory informs us that it is a strain that produces beta-lactamases with an extended spectrum. Which antibiotic, among the following, should be used?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: E. coli resistant to cephalosporins due to beta-lactamase production -> Need antibiotic with beta-lactamase inhibitor -> Amoxicillin clavulanic contains beta-lactamase inhibitor -> Amoxicillin clavulanic should be used -> 95%
CHAIN: E. coli resistant to cephalosporins due to beta-lactamase production -> Need antibiotic with broad spectrum coverage -> Ertapenem has broad spectrum coverage -> Ertapenem should be used -> 90%

CHAIN: E. coli resistant to cephalosporins due to beta-lactamase production -> Need antibiotic with beta-lactamase inhibitor -> Piperacillin/tazobactam contains beta-lactamase inhibitor -> Piperacillin/tazobactam should be used -> 85%
CHAIN: E. coli resistant to cephalosporins due to beta-lactamase production -> Ciprofloxacin is not effective against beta-lactamase-producing bacteria -> Ciprofloxacin should not be used -> 80%
analysis: Given the presence of E. coli resistant to cephalosporins producing beta-lactamases with an extended spectrum, the most appropriate antibiotic choice would be one that covers for this resistant strain. Ertapenem is a carbapenem antibiotic that is effective against ESBL-producing E. coli and would be the best choice in this scenario.
